tip: चार्ज हो रहा है (charge ho raha hai) = 'is getting charged' – हो (ho) for things happening on their own. If YOU charge it, that's चार्ज कर रहा हूँ (charge kar raha hoon).
You wait OF the bus, not for it: बस का इंतज़ार कर रहा हूँ (bus ka intezaar kar raha hoon = doing the bus's wait). इंतज़ार (intezaar) normally takes का.
फ़ोन करता हूँ (phone karta hoon) looks like 'I call' but means 'I'll call' – the simple present works as a right-away promise in Hindi.
'Can you understand' uses पाना: समझ पा रहे हैं (samajh paa rahe hain = managing to understand). पाना (paana) after a verb means 'manage to, succeed in'.
लग रहा है (lag raha hai) = 'is looking, seeming': चेहरा उतरा लग रहा है (chehra utra lag raha hai) = your face seems drawn. लगना (lagna) covers impressions.
'You should' starts with तुम्हें (tumhein = to you), not तुम (tum) – with चाहिए (chahiye), advice points at the person, so they take the to-form.
'Is prohibited' is just मना है (mana hai = is forbidden) after the plain verb: फ़ोटो खींचना मना है (photo kheenchna mana hai) – no 'it', no passive, nothing else needed.
Skills come to you in Hindi: तैरना आता है (tairna aata hai = swimming comes) means 'knows how to swim'. Learned abilities use आना (aana = to come), not सकना (sakna).
'Should have' just adds था: बोलना चाहिए था (bolna chahiye tha = should have spoken). The past marker sits after चाहिए, nothing else changes.
सक (sak) never stands alone – it glues onto the bare verb: बोल सकती है (bol sakti hai = can speak). English puts 'can' before the verb; Hindi attaches it after.
और (aur) usually means 'and', but after an amount it means 'more': दो सौ रुपये और (do sau rupaye aur) = two hundred rupees more.
No extra 'have to' word – करना है (karna hai = is to do) alone means must. The -ना (-na) verb form plus है (hai) carries the whole obligation.
Verb + के लिए (ke liye) means 'in order to': जाना (jaana = to go) shifts to जाने in जाने के लिए (jaane ke liye = in order to go).
पड़ेगा (padega) comes from पड़ना (padna = to fall): the duty falls on Nikhil, no choice in it. चाहिए (chahiye) suggests, पड़ना forces.
There is no verb 'need' here – चीनी चाहिए (cheeni chahiye) is literally 'sugar is wanted'. Noun + चाहिए = need; a verb before चाहिए means 'should'.
लेनी (leni), not लेना (lena) – the verb before चाहिए matches its object's gender: दवा (dava = medicine) is feminine, so 'to take' becomes लेनी.
After शायद (shayad = maybe), the verb often shifts to the maybe-form: आ सके (aa sake) rather than आ सकता है (aa sakta hai). Uncertainty can change the verb ending itself.
'Wants us to go' needs a full clause: चाहता है कि (chahta hai ki = wants that) + हम लखनऊ चलें (ham Lakhnau chalen = we go to Lucknow) – never an infinitive like English.
Impossibility is phrased 'from me': मुझसे (mujhse) + नहीं उठ पाएगा (nahin uth paega = won't get lifted) – the failure comes from your side, and the box बक्सा (baksa) is the subject.
करवाना (karvana) = get it done by someone else: एसी ठीक करवाना (AC theek karvana) is having it repaired, not repairing it yourself – that would be करना (karna).
'Try on' is wear-and-see: पहनकर देख (pahankar dekh = having worn, see). Hindi tests things by doing the action, then देखना (dekhna = to see).
सकना (sakna) also covers 'might': बारिश हो सकती है (barish ho sakti hai = rain can happen) means it might rain – possibility, not anyone's ability.
ख़ुदा हाफ़िज़ (khuda haafiz) – literally 'God (is your) protector', a goodbye from Urdu, common in everyday Hindi alongside नमस्ते (namaste).
Rekha is the subject, so 'her' homework is अपना (apna), not उसका (uska) – उसका would mean someone ELSE's homework, not her own.
In commands 'your' is अपना too: अपना पूरा नाम बताइए (apna poora naam bataiye) = tell your full name – the doer is 'you', so अपना points back at you.
अपना खाना ख़ुद बनाया (apna khaana khud banaya) – two self-words: अपना = his own (the food), ख़ुद = himself (did the cooking).
आपका अपना घर (aapka apna ghar) – अपना stacked after आपका means 'your very own'. A warm host formula: this house is yours too, not just ours.
अपनी-अपनी जगह (apni-apni jagah) – doubling अपना spreads it over everyone: each to their OWN place. Hindi repeats a word to mean each/respective.
अपनी माँ (apni maa) – अपना (apna) matches the thing owned, not the owner: माँ (maa) is feminine, so it's अपनी whether Lakshmi or her brother writes.
You don't miss things in Hindi – the memory comes to you: मुझे (mujhe = to me) + याद आती है (yaad aati hai = memory comes) = I miss my country.
